title: n8n vs Zapier vs Make: Which Automation Platform Should You Choose in 2026?
excerpt: A practical comparison of the three most popular automation platforms — when each one wins, where they fall short, and how to avoid the trap of picking the wrong one.
body:
Every automation project starts with the same question after the scope is defined: which platform runs it? The answer is not "the most popular one" — it is the one that matches your team's skills, your integration requirements, and your long-term maintenance capacity.

*Updated October 2026 — pricing and features checked against current plans.*

Here is how n8n, Zapier and Make actually compare when you look past the marketing pages. The big shift since last year: per-task pricing pain has pushed more teams toward self-hosted n8n, and AI steps (LLM calls inside workflows) are now a first-class feature on all three platforms — which changes the cost math again.

## The one-sentence version

- **Zapier** is the fastest way to connect two SaaS tools with a simple trigger-action flow, and the most expensive at scale.
- **Make** (formerly Integromat) gives you visual complexity — branching, error handling, and data transformation — at a lower price than Zapier.
- **n8n** is open-source, self-hostable, and the only one that lets you write custom code inline. It is the hardest to set up but the cheapest to run at volume.

## When to choose Zapier

Zapier wins when speed to first working automation matters more than cost or flexibility.

**Best for:**
- Teams with no engineering resources
- Simple two-step automations (trigger → action)
- Quick wins that prove automation value to stakeholders
- Organisations already invested in the Zapier ecosystem

**Reality check:**
- Pricing escalates fast. A 10-task zap runs 500 times a month on the free plan. The Starter plan ($29.99/mo) handles 750 tasks. At 2,000 tasks you are on the Professional plan ($73.50/mo). At 10,000 tasks, you are paying over $200/mo.
- Error handling is limited. When a zap fails, you get a notification and a retry — but no branching logic to handle the failure differently.
- Data transformation between steps is basic. If you need to reshape JSON or merge data from multiple sources, you hit limits quickly.

## When to choose Make

Make wins when you need visual complexity without writing code.

**Best for:**
- Teams that need branching logic and error paths
- Workflows with 5+ steps that need data transformation
- Budget-conscious teams outgrowing Zapier
- Organisations that want visual debugging (Make shows exactly where a scenario failed)

**Reality check:**
- The learning curve is steeper than Zapier. The visual builder is powerful but takes time to master.
- Some integrations are Make-specific and may not exist in Zapier's ecosystem.
- Self-hosting is not an option — you are on Make's cloud.
- Pricing is based on operations, not tasks. One scenario step can trigger multiple operations, so costs can surprise you.

## When to choose n8n

n8n wins when you need full control, custom logic, or cost efficiency at scale.

**Best for:**
- Engineering teams comfortable with code
- Workflows that need custom logic, API calls, or data processing
- High-volume automations where SaaS pricing becomes prohibitive
- Organisations with data residency or security requirements
- Teams that want to own their automation infrastructure

**Reality check:**
- Self-hosting requires DevOps capability. You need to manage the server, updates, and backups.
- The UI is functional but not as polished as Make or Zapier.
- Community nodes are great but variable in quality.
- The cloud version exists but is newer and less mature than the self-hosted option.

## The cost comparison that matters

Here is what a real-world automation costs on each platform at three volume levels:

| Monthly triggers | Zapier | Make | n8n (self-hosted) |
|-----------------|--------|------|--------------------|
| 500 | Free–$30 | Free–$10 | ~$10 (VPS cost) |
| 5,000 | $73–$150 | $30–$90 | ~$10–$20 |
| 50,000 | $400+ | $150–$300 | ~$20–$50 |

At 50,000 triggers per month, n8n costs roughly one-tenth of Zapier. That difference pays for an engineer's time to set it up.

## The integration question

All three platforms support the major SaaS tools: Slack, Google Workspace, HubSpot, Salesforce, Stripe, Shopify, and hundreds more. The differences are in the edges:

- **Zapier** has the largest integration library (6,000+ apps). If a SaaS tool has an API, Zapier probably has a built-in integration.
- **Make** has fewer pre-built integrations but compensates with a powerful HTTP module that can call any API directly.
- **n8n** has the fewest pre-built integrations but the most flexibility — you can write custom nodes in JavaScript/TypeScript, use the HTTP node for any API, and even run Python code inline.

## Our recommendation

Start with the platform that matches your current team, not your aspirational one:

1. **No engineers, simple needs?** Start with Zapier. Graduate to Make when complexity or cost demands it.
2. **Some technical skill, growing complexity?** Start with Make. The visual builder teaches automation thinking without requiring code.
3. **Engineering team, high volume, or security requirements?** Start with n8n. The upfront investment pays for itself within months.

The worst choice is picking the most powerful platform when your team cannot maintain it, or the simplest platform when your needs will outgrow it in six months.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is n8n really free?

Yes — the self-hosted edition is open-source and free. Your only cost is the server it runs on (a $10–$50/month VPS covers most workloads). n8n also sells a managed cloud plan, which is still far cheaper than Zapier at volume.

### Which is cheapest at high volume: n8n, Make or Zapier?

At tens of thousands of tasks per month, self-hosted n8n wins by an order of magnitude — see the cost table above. Make is the budget pick among fully-managed platforms; Zapier is the most expensive but the easiest to start with.

### Can n8n replace all my Zaps?

Almost always, yes. n8n has native nodes for the major SaaS tools, and anything with an API can be reached through its HTTP node or a custom JavaScript node. The migration audit is where we verify each integration before committing.

### Should a non-technical team use n8n?

Honestly? Probably not as the first choice. n8n rewards technical teams. Non-technical teams usually do better starting with Make, and moving to n8n later if volume justifies hiring or contracting the expertise.
